title: Jonathan Edwards
hookLine: the Great Awakening in New England, and Edwards writing on religious affections

cards: Honey on the tongue. You can read that honey is sweet, repeat it, pass a test on it. Or you can taste it.
Same fact, two different kinds of knowing. A pastor in a small New England town used that picture, the taste of honey, to describe faith.
Then his own church was stirred up: people weeping, staying up late to pray, crowding his study with questions. Some neighbors called it a work of God. Others called it hysteria.
He decided the honest thing was to sit down and think it through.

teach.h: HOW DO YOU TELL WHAT IS REAL?
teach.b: Jonathan Edwards was a Congregationalist minister in Northampton, Massachusetts, during the season of revival people later called the Great Awakening, the same stirring Whitefield preached into.

He's often remembered for one frightening sermon about sinners in the hands of an angry God. But much of his life went into a harder question: when a revival sweeps through a town, how do you tell what is real?
He answered in a long book, A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections.

Its claim is short: "True religion, in great part, consists in holy affections." By affections he didn't mean passing moods. He meant the deep leanings of the heart: what a person loves, hates, hopes for and delights in.
In a sermon on a divine and supernatural light, he drew the difference that gives us our line.

There's believing, as a matter of opinion, that God is holy and gracious, and there's having a sense of the heart, tasting it, the way someone who has eaten honey knows its sweetness as a reader never will.
Edwards warned that strong feelings prove nothing on their own. Tears, shaking, loud joy: none of them, he argued, settle whether something is from God.

The chief sign, he wrote, is a changed life, the fruit of the heart showing up in ordinary practice, day after day. So he defended the feelings against the scoffers, and tested them against the enthusiasts.
A sense of the heart, yes. Then watch what it does on Monday.

how: Edwards is read in Reformed, Presbyterian, Baptist and evangelical churches and seminaries, and his Religious Affections is still used by pastors trying to tell real spiritual awakening from passing excitement.

games.q: you're a pastor and your town is swept by weeping, late-night prayer and fierce argument. some say it's God, some say it's hysteria. what do you do?
o: shut it down to keep the peace.
think it through and test it by what it changes.
celebrate every strong feeling as proof.
games.why: Edwards wrote a long book on it, defending the feelings against scoffers and testing them against enthusiasts: the chief sign is a changed life.

practice: Sit, breathe slowly, and ask quietly: what am I leaning toward right now, and what am I leaning away from? Don't fix anything; just name it the way you'd name a taste: wanting, dreading, delighting, longing.
If you pray, hold what you find before God without dressing it up; if you don't, simply notice the leaning.

wordCard.voice: Jonathan Edwards. A New England pastor in the Great Awakening who wrote that true religion lives in holy affections, and that a changed life is the best test of them.
